content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Array indices and contiguous sequence models is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. An array maps integer positions to ordered values; valid indices form the half-open range from zero to length.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Array indices and contiguous sequence models, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Traversal and loop invariants
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Traversal and loop invariants within a constrained data-processing problem.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Traversal and loop invariants to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Traversal and loop invariants is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. During left-to-right traversal, define what has been proven about the processed prefix before advancing the boundary.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Traversal and loop invariants, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use states, operations, invariants, diagrams, and complexity bounds. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Traversal and loop invariants
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state

core_concepts.rule: A linked list is a chain of nodes; each next reference preserves reachability and the tail terminates with no successor.

core_concepts.title: Linked-list traversal and search
core_concepts.rule: Traversal follows links rather than numeric indices and must stop at the end or when the target is found.

core_concepts.title: Insertion and deletion by rewiring
core_concepts.rule: Local list changes update a small set of links, but only after preserving references to the remaining chain.

core_concepts.title: Fast and slow pointer reasoning
core_concepts.rule: Pointers moving at different rates reveal middle positions or cycles through relative-distance invariants.

core_concepts.title: Stacks and last-in-first-out
core_concepts.rule: A stack exposes only the most recently added unremoved item, supporting nested and reversal processes.

core_concepts.title: Queues and first-in-first-out
core_concepts.rule: A queue removes items in arrival order and needs separate front and rear state for efficient operations.

core_concepts.title: Deques and monotonic queues
core_concepts.rule: A deque supports both ends; a monotonic deque discards dominated candidates while preserving useful order.

core_concepts.title: Selecting linear structures
core_concepts.rule: Choose arrays, lists, stacks, queues, or deques from required access position, update pattern, order, and complexity.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Nodes, links, and list invariants is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. A linked list is a chain of nodes; each next reference preserves reachability and the tail terminates with no successor.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Nodes, links, and list invariants, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Fast and slow pointer reasoning
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Fast and slow pointer reasoning within a constrained data-processing problem.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Fast and slow pointer reasoning to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Fast and slow pointer reasoning is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Pointers moving at different rates reveal middle positions or cycles through relative-distance invariants.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Fast and slow pointer reasoning, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Linked Lists, Stacks and Queues: Data-Structure Reasoning Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a constrained data-processing problem that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate data-structure reasoning portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Linked Lists, Stacks and Queues. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A linked list is a chain of nodes; each next reference preserves reachability and the tail terminates with no successor.
Traversal follows links rather than numeric indices and must stop at the end or when the target is found.
Local list changes update a small set of links, but only after preserving references to the remaining chain.
Pointers moving at different rates reveal middle positions or cycles through relative-distance invariants.
A stack exposes only the most recently added unremoved item, supporting nested and reversal processes.
A queue removes items in arrival order and needs separate front and rear state for efficient operations.

core_concepts.title: Key-value and membership models
core_concepts.rule: A map associates unique keys with values, while a set records only whether a key is present.

core_concepts.title: Hash functions and bucket placement
core_concepts.rule: A hash function deterministically maps a key to a numeric code used to select a bounded bucket.

core_concepts.title: Collisions and equality
core_concepts.rule: Different keys can share a bucket, so collision handling must still use correct key equality to distinguish them.

core_concepts.title: Load factor and resizing
core_concepts.rule: As entries per bucket rise, expected operation cost worsens; resizing expands capacity and redistributes entries.

core_concepts.title: Frequency maps and counting invariants
core_concepts.rule: After processing a prefix, each stored value equals the exact number of times its key appeared in that prefix.

core_concepts.title: Grouping and indexing by derived keys
core_concepts.rule: A derived canonical key can group records that share a property, such as normalized letters or category.

core_concepts.title: Memoization and cached subproblems
core_concepts.rule: Memoization maps a complete subproblem state to its solved result, avoiding repeated work without changing correctness.

core_concepts.title: Hash-structure trade-offs
core_concepts.rule: Expected constant-time lookup depends on good hashing, while ordering, worst-case needs, memory, and key mutability may favor another structure.

lessons.title: Key-value and membership models
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Key-value and membership models within a constrained data-processing problem.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Key-value and membership models to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Key-value and membership models is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A map associates unique keys with values, while a set records only whether a key is present.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Key-value and membership models, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use states, operations, invariants, diagrams, and complexity bounds. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Frequency maps and counting invariants is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. After processing a prefix, each stored value equals the exact number of times its key appeared in that prefix.

content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Frequency maps and counting invariants, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Hash Maps, Hash Sets and Frequency Structures: Data-Structure Reasoning Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a constrained data-processing problem that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate data-structure reasoning portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Hash Maps, Hash Sets and Frequency Structures. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A map associates unique keys with values, while a set records only whether a key is present.
A hash function deterministically maps a key to a numeric code used to select a bounded bucket.
Different keys can share a bucket, so collision handling must still use correct key equality to distinguish them.
As entries per bucket rise, expected operation cost worsens; resizing expands capacity and redistributes entries.
After processing a prefix, each stored value equals the exact number of times its key appeared in that prefix.
A derived canonical key can group records that share a property, such as normalized letters or category.
Memoization maps a complete subproblem state to its solved result, avoiding repeated work without changing correctness.
Expected constant-time lookup depends on good hashing, while ordering, worst-case needs, memory, and key mutability may favor another structure.

Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps: Data-Structure Reasoning Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a constrained data-processing problem that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate data-structure reasoning portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A tree has one root and unique parent paths; every subtree is itself a tree with smaller scope.
Depth-first traversal follows a branch before siblings, while breadth-first traversal processes nodes by distance from the root.
Every node partitions keys so left-subtree values precede it and right-subtree values follow it under the chosen ordering rule.
Operations follow the ordering invariant; deletion reconnects subtrees while preserving every remaining key's order.
Keeping subtree heights controlled prevents an ordered tree from degenerating into a linear chain.
A binary heap combines complete-tree shape with parent priority, guaranteeing fast access to one extreme rather than full order.
A priority queue repeatedly exposes the highest- or lowest-priority item; a bounded heap can retain the best k candidates.
Select a tree, BST, heap, or flat structure according to hierarchy, ordered lookup, priority access, update cost, and memory.

content_blocks.body: Advanced structure selection is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Choose representations by operation mix, density, ordering, connectivity, prefix needs, guarantees, and implementation cost.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Advanced structure selection, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use states, operations, invariants, diagrams, and complexity bounds. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Advanced structure selection
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Choose representations by operation mix, density, ordering, connectivity, prefix needs, guarantees, and implementation cost.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Advanced structure selection.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Advanced structure selection' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.

lessons.summary: Advanced structure selection is mastered when the learner can model its inputs and state, apply the rule 'Choose representations by operation mix, density, ordering, connectivity, prefix needs, guarantees, and implementation cost.', and prove the result with normal, boundary, and rejected traces.

project.title: Graphs, Tries and Advanced Structures: Data-Structure Reasoning Portfolio
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a constrained data-processing problem that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate data-structure reasoning portfolio that demonstrates all eight skills from Graphs, Tries and Advanced Structures. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A graph models entities and relationships; adjacency lists favor sparse edges while matrices favor constant-time edge checks.
BFS or DFS expands reachable vertices while a visited set ensures each vertex is finalized according to the traversal rule.
BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing edge distance, so the first discovery gives a shortest unweighted path.
A topological order places every directed prerequisite before its dependent and exists only when there is no directed cycle.
Relaxation improves a best-known distance when an edge offers a cheaper route; algorithm choice depends on weight properties.
Union-find maintains partitions under union and connectivity queries using representative parents, path compression, and rank or size.
A trie shares prefixes along root-to-node paths, trading memory for operations proportional to key length.
Choose representations by operation mix, density, ordering, connectivity, prefix needs, guarantees, and implementation cost.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 5 supplies only constraints, acceptance criteria, and review checkpoints.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Graph vertices, edges, and representations and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Graph traversal and visited invariants and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Shortest paths in unweighted graphs and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Directed acyclic graphs and topological order and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Weighted paths and relaxation and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Disjoint sets and connectivity and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Tries and prefix structure and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Advanced structure selection and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

maximum documented size
duplicate or retry

malformed or unauthorized input

Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.

Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

optional_mastery_challenge.title: Optional Mastery Transfer
optional_mastery_challenge.prompt: Transfer the level's eight governing rules to a new version of a constrained data-processing problem with one changed constraint, one new failure state, and one stricter evidence requirement.
required_outputs: change-impact table across all eight skills
normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery traces
success_criteria: The changed constraint is applied consistently.
No unaffected invariant is silently removed.
The new failure state has visible recovery behavior.
Evidence distinguishes old and new behavior.
